statement: Different numbers are chosen from 1 to 10. How many must be chosen to be certain that two of them add to 11?

choices.misconception: I assumed the first two chosen would pair up, which is possible but not certain.
I counted the pairs that add to 11 and gave that count rather than one more.
I assumed every number had to be chosen before a pair was guaranteed.
I added one to the ten numbers rather than to the five pairs.

hints: Group the numbers into the pairs that add to eleven.
The ten numbers split into pairs summing to 11. Choosing at most one from each pair avoids a match, so the answer is one more than the number of pairs.
The pairs are 1 with 10, 2 with 9, 3 with 8, 4 with 7 and 5 with 6.

solutions.reliable: The numbers fall into the five pairs 1 and 10, 2 and 9, 3 and 8, 4 and 7, 5 and 6. Five numbers can avoid a pair by taking one from each, but a sixth must complete one, so six is needed. The transferable idea: build the pigeonholes out of the forbidden condition itself, then take one more than the number of holes.
solutions.elegant: Five holes and six items settles it with no case checking at all.

whyOnTest: Pigeonhole arguments in the 5-point block turn on finding the right pigeonholes, and the count of holes is always offered instead of the answer.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
